headline: GitHub added 4 million CPU cores and 160PB storage to handle AI-generated code surge
summary: The world's largest code repository saw commits grow sixfold and merged pull requests jump 4x, driven by agentic AI, necessitating a massive infrastructure upgrade.
details: GitHub significantly scaled its infrastructure, adding 4 million CPU cores, 160 petabytes of storage, and 50 Tb/s of networking capacity. This massive expansion was required to keep pace with an unprecedented influx of AI-generated code.

Raw repository activity has seen a dramatic year-over-year increase. Code commits, which involve adding or removing code, grew sixfold, while merged pull requests, finalizing features or bug fixes, jumped fourfold.

The growth pattern is exponential: monthly commits rose from 1.4 billion in April to 2.9 billion in August, and then to 7.4 billion by September. GitHub recorded 17.9 billion code pushes in the past 12 months alone.

Agentic AI is identified as the primary driver behind this dizzying rise in code volume. By last September, over 40% of all pull requests were initiated by an agent, a substantial increase from 17% in March.

Furthermore, repositories that begin with AI-generated code typically exhibit eight times the activity compared to those developed entirely by human hands. This highlights AI's accelerating impact on development cycles.

This surge in code activity places disproportionate strain on Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines. Each commit or pull request triggers numerous actions, including linting, and running extensive code and integration tests.

The ballooning hardware requirements for these processes demanded massive amounts of computing power and I/O. GitHub even had to reengineer its backend to decouple storage from compute as much as possible to manage the escalating demand.

headline_marked: MIT Tech Review: [[AI agents need real-time monitoring]] to avoid 'flying blind'
headline: MIT Tech Review: AI agents need real-time monitoring to avoid 'flying blind'
summary: Current AI agent deployments lack adequate oversight, leading to a 'flying blind' scenario. Experts advocate for urgent real-time monitoring to ensure safe and effective operation.
details: MIT Technology Review highlights a critical oversight in the deployment of AI agents: a lack of real-time monitoring. Currently, developers and users are "flying blind," unable to fully track the actions and decisions of these autonomous systems.

This absence of visibility poses significant risks, as AI agents operate with increasing independence across various domains. Without proper oversight, understanding their behavior, identifying unintended consequences, or intervening when necessary becomes challenging.

The publication emphasizes the urgent need for robust monitoring mechanisms. These systems would provide continuous feedback on AI agent operations, allowing for immediate detection of anomalies or deviations from intended goals.

Implementing real-time monitoring is crucial for ensuring accountability, safety, and ethical deployment of AI technologies. It would enable better control and understanding of complex AI systems as they become more integrated into daily life.
